articles.title: Timestral: Mistral's time-series foundation models
articles.text: Timestral, Mistral’s first family of time-series foundation models, delivers state-of-the-art probabilistic, multivariate forecasts with just 209M parameters, outperforming larger models on key benchmarks while supporting past and future covariates. Available in four sizes (5M to 209M parameters), it balances accuracy and efficiency, running efficiently on CPUs and excelling in zero-shot forecasting for diverse domains. The model combines synthetic pre-training, covariate-aware attention, and long-context learning, with fine-tuning options for domain adaptation via Mistral Forge.Today, we’re releasing Timestral, our first family of time-series foundation models. Our largest model, at just 209M parameters, ranks first on all three of the field's main public benchmarks, GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, outperforming the previous state of the art with only two-thirds of the model parameters.Timestral delivers probabilistic, multivariate forecasts and supports past-only and known-future covariates. Our family of models sits on the Pareto front of forecasting accuracy versus model size, delivering leading performance at each size. Results have been submitted to the GIFT-Eval and TIME leaderboards.Time Series Foundation Models (TSFM)Time series is one of the most common data types in enterprise, from sensor telemetry to observability metrics. Forecasts built on it drive decisions in capacity planning, energy, supply chains, risk and maintenance.Industrial plants forecast process sensors against the production schedule, catch equipment drift before it fails, and plan capacity and spare parts across thousands of assets. Finance teams forecast flows, volumes, and volatility to inform positions, hedging, and treasury across thousands of accounts.Classical models such as ARIMA and linear regression remain well-established tools for forecasting time series. These models are usually fitted to a single series and learn only from that series' history.Deep learning models such as PatchTST add the capacity to learn nonlinear patterns across many related series, but they are still typically trained from scratch on each dataset, so what they learn doesn't carry over to new domains.Time series foundation models bring the pre-training approach to time series. Trained on a large and diverse corpus, our model learns patterns that transfer across series, forecasting zero-shot on data it has never seen, even in domains where data is scarce.Benchmark ResultsWe evaluated Timestral on the three main public forecasting benchmarks: GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench. Among pre-trained, zero-shot models, it ranks first across all five metrics. These results come from a single checkpoint, without ensembling.GIFT-Eval, top ten of 83 comparable pretrained and zero-shot entries. Lower is better.TIME, top ten of the 35 leaderboard entries. Lower is better on both metrics.fev-bench, top ten of the 37 leaderboard entries, by SQL skill score. Higher is better.Family of models optimised for every specificationTimestral has been optimised as a family of four models: 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M parameters. The larger models improve forecast performance, while the smaller ones are faster and cheaper. All four share the same architecture and training recipe. Every size sits on the Pareto front of accuracy versus model size: for each model size, no public model forecasts better.Score vs model size on GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench (shown as 1 − skill score). Lower is better. Our 28M model beats Chronos-2, about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME. Our 209M model beats TimesFM-3 and Falcon-2.0 with fewer parameters.Timestral does not need a GPU at inference. On a standard server CPU with 8 threads, forecasting one day ahead from three weeks of 15-minute history takes 10 ms with the 5M model and 140 ms with the 209M model. Smaller models trade some accuracy for speed: the 28M model is five times faster than the 209M model, and the 123M model comes within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its latency.An industrial exampleConsider an industrial plant with thousands of sensors across its equipment. Timestral can improve the forecasts on that data in several ways.Multivariate forecasting. A pump's vibration, temperature and pressure don't move independently. A rise in one often explains or causes a change in another. Timestral models related series jointly, so it can use those dependencies instead of forecasting each sensor in isolation.Probabilistic forecasting. A single predicted value may not show the full picture. Timestral predicts a full set of quantiles, so teams can see how wide the uncertainty is, set alert thresholds that reflect it, and plan maintenance around risk rather than a single number.Categorical covariates. Some covariates take values from a set of categories rather than continuous numbers, such as the day of the week, or a machine's state (running, idle, under maintenance). Encoding these as numbers would impose an order or scale they don't have. Timestral takes them as categorical inputs directly to improve forecasts.Known-future covariates. Some drivers of sensor behaviour are known in advance, such as production schedules, planned shutdowns, weather forecasts. Timestral can condition on them to improve forecast quality, so a scheduled load increase is expected rather than flagged as a surprise.From Model to SystemTimestral is a numerical model that can run inside existing monitoring pipelines, or be paired with our language models in multi-modal agentic workflows.In the plant, that could look like this:Timestral running continuously on the plant's sensor streams, detecting anomalies as they occur.When it flags an anomaly on a pump, an agent embeds the signals and compares against embeddings of past sensor data to find similar historical failures.The agent then starts sub-agents to run a root cause analysis, drawing on context from that plant, such as maintenance records, shift logs and operator notes, equipment manuals, past work orders, and readings from related equipment.The agent drafts a suggested diagnosis based on the findings, with supporting evidence and possible next steps.The plant manager gets a diagnosis and a plan backed by the sensor data, rather than just an alert.Key technical contributionsSeveral ideas have been combined to produce these results. Each will be described in detail in the technical report.Decoupled Horizon Forecasting. Causal decoders trained with contiguous patch masking, as in Toto 2.0 and TimesFM-3, mask out the values to be forecast, so they look like missing values and are also lost as context for later forecasts. Our approach, DHF, separates the two: the full history stays in the sequence, and learned forecast tokens read the history before them. Every observed value thus serves as both target and context, true gaps stay flagged as missing, and training horizon lengths and missing-data augmentation can be tuned independently of each other.Covariate-aware attention. Each input series is assigned a role: target variate, past-only covariate or known-future covariate. Known-future covariates are visible across the whole window while targets stay causal, and information flows only from covariates to targets. Timestral can therefore use a holiday calendar or a weather forecast without leaking a target's own future into its forecast.Synthetic-first data. The majority of the training data was synthetic. We first generated univariate processes with coherent temporal dynamics, including trends, seasonality and diverse noise patterns. We then used a multivariate synthesizer to construct multivariate series by introducing nonlinear dependencies between these processes.Two-stage training. Timestral is first pre-trained at scale on purely synthetic data with context size 8192, then post-trained on a mix of real and synthetic data with a 4x longer context. The objective is a pinball loss over 21 quantiles, a discrete approximation of CRPS.A model that can be adaptedPublic benchmarks measure general performance, but production data can be significantly different in behavior and structure. It may also shift over time as markets change regime, equipment degrades and demand patterns move. The lasting value lies in being able to adapt a model to in-domain data and keep retraining it as the distribution moves.For organisations that want to go further, Timestral is available through Mistral Forge, the same training pipeline we use for our language models. It supports:Zero-shot inference out of the box.Architectural extensions, such as domain-specific covariates.Fine-tuning on proprietary data, specialising to a domain while preserving general performance.Control over the training data, including adjusting the training mix, replaying pre-training data, and generating synthetic data samples to reflect the target domain. Full control over the data ensures that nothing we backtest was seen during pre-training.The full pipeline can be deployed on our clients’ hardware, including air-gapped environments.What’s nextWe have published a GitHub repository so you can run Timestral on your own data. A technical report with the full results will follow. For more specialised forecasting problems, or to collaborate on research, please reach out to us.TimestralTypeTime-series foundation model (TSFM)Parameters5M, 28M, 123M and 209MContext length32,768 time stepsOutputProbabilistic forecasts, 21 quantilesInputsMultivariate targets, past-only and known-future covariatesDeploymentOn-prem, VPC or air-gappedLicenceModified MIT

articles.sourceTitle: CERN and Mistral sign a statement of intent to establish a strategic partnership
articles.title: CERN and Mistral join forces to accelerate AI for science – Home
articles.text:
CERN, the European Laboratory for Particle Physics, and Mistral, a European developer of large-scale AI models, have signed a statement of intent to establish a long-term strategic partnership focused on developing foundation models for scientific discovery.

The partnership brings together CERN’s expertise in fundamental physics, scientific data and large-scale computing with Mistral’s leadership in large-scale model training, leveraging these combined capabilities and resources to advance AI for science on an exceptional scale. While the initial focus is on high-energy physics, the partnership has the potential to contribute to the development of AI approaches that can serve the broader scientific community.

At the heart of this work is the ambition to develop a single pretrained Large Physics Model – the first foundation model for collider physics. It will be trained on billions of simulated proton-proton collisions at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the world’s largest and most powerful particle accelerator, and designed to support multiple tasks, from reconstructing particle collisions and identifying particles to flagging unexpected signals and evaluating future detector designs.

The model is intended to address a fundamental challenge in analysing LHC collisions. Today, reconstruction relies on a chain of specialised algorithms that progressively transform detector signals into the particles and other objects used for physics analysis. Machine learning has long played an important role in this process, improving performance across a range of specialised tasks. Foundation models offer the potential to build on these advances, learning across the whole reconstruction chain and supporting multiple tasks within a single model.

“High-energy physics provides a unique environment in which artificial intelligence can be developed and tested with exceptional rigour. We are partnering with Mistral, a leading European AI company, to advance AI capabilities that can serve the whole physics community and be shared,” said Enrica Porcari, CERN’s Chief Information Officer.

CERN is home to one of the world’s largest volumes of scientific data, with around one exabyte – one million terabytes – of experimental data from the LHC stored to date. The number of collisions is set to increase tenfold with the HL-LHC, which is expected to begin operation around 2030. This combination of scale and scientific precision provides exceptional conditions for developing and testing AI.

“We are proud to work with CERN to explore what large-scale AI models can bring to the growing complexity of particle physics. Together, we have the opportunity to push the frontiers of high-energy physics, developing AI capabilities that have the potential to lead to new scientific discoveries,” said Johannes Brandstetter, Vice-President of AI for Engineering at Mistral.

By bringing together European excellence in AI and fundamental science, this partnership marks a step towards a new generation of AI tools capable of addressing the scale, precision and complexity of modern science in Europe and beyond.

About Mistral:

Mistral is a global AI lab building state-of-the-art open-weight models, products and infrastructure that enable enterprises, public institutions and advanced industries to own, customise and control their AI. Headquartered in France, Mistral has a strong international presence across Europe, North America and Asia.

For more information, visit www.mistral.ai.

articles.sourceTitle: Show HN: Qwen3-4B with the AI writing tics trained out
articles.title: Qwen3-4B with the AI writing tics trained out
articles.text:
just you

Qwen3-4B with the AI writing tics trained out
A small open model, fine-tuned on a MacBook Air, that writes without em dashes, "not X, but Y" or lists of three and needs no system prompt, and you can run it locally with Ollama.

TL;DR

I trained the assistant writing habits out of Qwen3-4B-Instruct and released it as qwen3-4b-deslop. With Ollama it's ollama run hf.co/erikkannike/qwen3-4b-deslop-v4-GGUF:Q4_K_M, a 2.5 GB download.
On 40 prompts it never saw in training, the slop score dropped from 121 to 12.5 per 1000 words, and 68% of answers score in the range of human writing. Em dashes went from 20.5 per 1000 words to zero.
It still answers 30 of 30 factual questions correctly and fits the requested genre and length as often as the original. Its predictions on human-written prose moved about a third as much as with runtime steering.
An intermediate version scored 9.9 and wrote badly: opinion pieces without an opinion, invented studies, and a new habit of joining every sentence with ", which". Fixing that took a second filter that checks whether an answer does what the prompt asked.
The voice is plain to the point of flat, and it still invents names and places.

My home lab is a MacBook Air, so this is a 4B model trained on 161 answers. The recipe doesn't depend on the model size, and running it on larger models is the next step.

Answers on 40 held-out prompts
These are one sampled answer per prompt from the original model and from the released one, on ten topics in four genres, with no system prompt. Underlined passages are what the slop detector counts.

Topic

Original Qwen3-4B-Instruct
De-slopped

Generation stopped at 260 tokens, so long answers end mid-sentence. Hover an underlined passage to see which habit it is. The scores are per 1000 words; human writing usually scores under 15.

The slop score
The score comes from a detector I wrote from a style guide of AI writing habits: the em dash, "it's not X, it's Y", lists of three, rhetorical questions answered on the spot, signposts like "here's the thing", short fragments for emphasis, and words like "delve" and "seamless". Each habit has a weight, and the score is a weighted count per 1000 words. A paragraph by a careful human writer scores close to zero, and the original model averages 121.
A regex can't tell good writing from bad, so every model below was also checked for damage. Drift measures how far its predictions on 22 passages of human prose move from the original model's. A 30-question quiz checks that it still knows things, and a rule-based check flags broken output like lowercase sentence starts or a lost topic. I also read a sample of answers from every model.

Training method
An earlier experiment on this model found the assistant register as a direction inside it: subtracting it while the model writes, together with a plain-style system prompt, takes the score to about 15, but it needs the prompt and code running during generation, and it shifts the model's predictions on ordinary text. A second one read neurons one at a time and found four whose sign flip removes 70% of "not X, but Y" at almost no cost, though only for that one habit.
To get both into the weights I used distillation: a teacher, built from whatever worked best so far, answers 288 training prompts. I keep the answers that pass the checks, and a small LoRA adapter learns to produce them from the bare prompt. The first round got the score to about 20 with no prompt and no hooks.

Round two
For round two the teacher was the round-one model plus the four-neuron patch and the plain-style prompt. Adding the direction steering on top as well produced the lowest score I have measured, 9.5, from text with no capital letters that wandered off topic, so I took the steering back out. The teacher then averaged 7.4, and the student trained on its 171 best answers scored 9.9, with 80% of answers in the human range.
In its answers, an opinion piece about a company's new CRM never took a position and read like an incident report. A blog post about moving to a new city became a third-person story about a family with a leaking apartment. A piece about houseplants cited "a study from the University of Technology Sydney", which the model invented. Almost every sentence ran into the next with ", which" or ", so", 28 times as often as in the original model. That last habit came from my own teacher prompt, which had told the model to join sentences "with because, so, but, which", and two rounds of imitation had amplified it.
Task-fit checks
I added rule-based checks for whether an answer does what the prompt asked. An opinion piece has to state a position early, a personal reflection has to be in the first person, an email has to open with a greeting, and the length has to roughly match the request. Two more checks count ", which" and ", so" joins and invented studies and percentages. On those, the round-two model did what was asked only 60% of the time, against 78% for the original.

Round three
The third teacher got a prompt that put the task first: take a position when asked, write in the first person when it's personal, vary the sentences, and don't invent studies or names. It wrote three answers per prompt, and an answer was kept only if it scored under 12, passed the damage checks and passed all the task checks. About 30% did, which covered 161 of the 288 prompts.
The model trained on those answers is the released one. Its score rose a little, from 9.9 to 12.5, while task fit went back to 80% and the ", which" joins fell from 1.4 to 0.3 per 100 words. Invented studies and percentages nearly disappeared.

Rate per 1000 words on the 40 held-out prompts, original model against the released one.

Downloads and usage
The quantised build (Q4_K_M, 2.5 GB) runs on a laptop with Ollama or llama.cpp:
ollama run hf.co/erikkannike/qwen3-4b-deslop-v4-GGUF:Q4_K_M
llama-cli -hf erikkannike/qwen3-4b-deslop-v4-GGUF:Q4_K_M
The full-precision weights load with transformers like any Qwen3-4B checkpoint:
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
name = "erikkannike/qwen3-4b-deslop-v4"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name, torch_dtype="auto")
msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": "Write a LinkedIn post about switching to a four-day week."}]
ids = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt")
out = model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=300, do_sample=True, temperature=0.7)
print(tok.decode(out[0][ids.shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True))
The repo also has the parts on their own: the LoRA adapter (126 MB) and the neuron edit, a 175-byte list of four weight columns and their scales. The adapter was trained with the edit active, so the two go together.

Limitations
The voice is flat: the model writes runs of short declarative sentences, and its personal pieces read like diary entries.
It also still makes things up: studies and percentages are rare now, but invented names and places are common, like a coffee shop on Maple Street run by a woman named Maria, because concrete detail is what every round rewarded. It also runs long, and answers to "about 150 words" often come in near 200.
I have only tested short English prose in these genres. Code, long conversations, other languages and tool use may be no better than the original model, or worse. The score is my style guide written as regular expressions, and no blind test with readers has checked it yet. The numbers also move between runs: the same model scored 10.2 through the adapter and 12.5 as merged weights, from sampling differences alone.

Next steps
Each student ended up about as good as the best answers its teacher could write, so a better model needs a better teacher. I'm putting together a set of excellent human writing, public-domain essays and letters plus modern pieces, to use as examples for a base model. A base model never went through assistant training and still writes like the people it learned from. If that teacher writes better than this model does, the same recipe should produce a student with some taste as well as clean habits. After that comes the same pipeline on a 7 to 8B model and one around 30B, and a blind test where people pick the better text.

Method notes and caveats

Base model: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 in bf16. Every adapter is a rank-16 LoRA on all attention and MLP projections, trained for two epochs on the bare user prompt with loss on the response only, between one and three hours per round on an M2 MacBook Air.
Test set: ten topics never used in training, each in four genres (blog post, LinkedIn post, explainer, opinion piece), one sampled answer per prompt at temperature 0.7, no system prompt. Drift is the KL divergence from the original model on 22 passages of human prose.
The task-fit checks are simple rules (a stance word near the start of an opinion piece, first-person pronouns in a reflection, a greeting in an email, word counts) and they miss things a reader would catch. The training data was filtered on the same checks reported here, so the task-fit numbers flatter the model somewhat.
The neuron edit flips the sign of four MLP neurons (layer 32 neuron 4852, layer 33 neuron 348, layer 28 neuron 1121, layer 32 neuron 5418), which is the same as negating four columns of their layers' down-projection weights. The GGUF build was quantised from a Q8_0 conversion of the merged weights.
The readers' chat and live cursors connect readers directly over WebRTC (Trystero with public Nostr relays). Peers can see each other's IP addresses, nothing is saved, and "hide" disconnects you.

articles.sourceTitle: Hybrid Reasoning Agents: LLM agents that think in latent space, act through text
articles.title: [2610.18861] Hybrid Reasoning Agents
articles.text:
Computer Science > Computation and Language

arXiv:2610.18861 (cs)

Title:Hybrid Reasoning Agents

View a PDF of the paper titled Hybrid Reasoning Agents, by Jiaru Zou and 7 other authors
View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract:How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at this https URL.

articles.title: Investing in the public benefit \ Anthropic
articles.text: Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company.The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as a wholly-owned LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.
